Akzent / a comparison notebook

A consonant remembers an accent

A local snapshot of the learner's rule, fixed predictions, source citations, and fictional-word experiment. All fonts and seven complete source pages are embedded. This file makes no network requests.

The current rule

After an accented syllable: þ; after an unaccented syllable: d.

The target is an older medial t in a voiced environment. Sanskrit accent is comparative evidence; Sanskrit is not Gothic's ancestor. Gothic d and þ are spellings, not a complete phonetic transcription.

Current rule against revealed observations
MeaningSanskrit comparisonPredictionGothic observationResult
fatherpitár-dfadarAgrees
brotherbhrā́tar-þbrōþarAgrees
otherántara-þanþarAgrees
under / withinantárdundarAgrees

Predictions kept at the time of testing

  1. Prediction 1: under / within

    After an accented syllable: þ; after an unaccented syllable: þ. Predicted þ; observed undar.

  2. Prediction 2: under / within

    After an accented syllable: þ; after an unaccented syllable: d. Predicted d; observed undar.

  3. Prediction 3: which of two

    After an accented syllable: þ; after an unaccented syllable: d. Predicted d; observed hvaþar.

Changing the current rule does not revise these earlier records.

My explanation

My first prediction gave þ for ‘under’; Gothic undar has d. Changing the unaccented case to d explains that row and the starting pair. The comparison ántara- / anþar beside antár / undar is useful because a similar n-t sequence accompanies two accent positions. The rule agrees with six of these eight selected observations. Sanskrit katará- still predicts d where Gothic hvaþar has þ. Greek πότερος has a different accent; Sanskrit is evidence, not an unchanged copy of the ancestral language. The compound member -fadi- also needs a compound-accent account before I can treat páti- as its exact accent comparison. I have not proved such an account. In Verner’s fictional word, the third accent protects θ while the other medial fricatives voice. Moving accent to the first syllable afterwards preserves that contrast; moving it before voicing loses the contrast. This is an experiment on the explanation, not an independent historical date. The saved environment test also shows why an accented predecessor blocks voicing. Working backwards, I kept g / z / þ and allowed either event order. Only the third old accent fits. By contrast h / z / d would permit every old accent when the order is unknown: fixing the accent early erases the distinction before voicing. This inverse result concerns the fictional word, not a recovered lexical accent.

Cited readings: What actually conditions the sound?; A rule has to travel beyond its first examples; Keep the resistant evidence.

Verner's invented word

All forms in this experiment are hypothetical. An asterisk indicates an unattested form; it does not make this particular invented word a reconstruction of an actual lexical item. The stages below isolate consonants and accent, not the entire development of Gothic.

  1. Older accent*akasátam

    A fictional input; the selected accent has not moved.

  2. Medial voicing*aɣazáθam

    Only the fricative immediately after the old accent stays voiceless.

  3. Later accent*áɣazaθam

    Moving the accent now does not undo the consonant differences.

  4. Verner’s spelling*agazaþ(am)

    His hypothetical Gothic endpoint; (am) brackets the ending.

The displayed event order is an instructional intervention on Verner's explanation. A real language cannot be rerun, and this experiment is not independent evidence dating the historical changes.

German readings with new English

Selected excerpts are normalized, not diplomatic transcriptions. þ replaces the historical dental type; an ellipsis in the fictional-word excerpt omits his phonetic notation. Sanskrit forms elsewhere use modern IAST.

What actually conditions the sound? / p. 114 / cited

die so entstandenen tonlosen fricativae nebst der vom indogermanischen ererbten tonlosen fricativa s wurden weiter inlautend bei tönender nachbarschaft selbst tönend, erhielten sich aber als tonlose im nachlaute betonter silben.

The voiceless fricatives that had arisen in this way, together with the voiceless fricative s inherited from Indo-European, further became voiced themselves inside a word in a voiced environment, but remained voiceless after accented syllables.

tonlosen / tönend
Voiceless / voiced. These refer to vocal-fold vibration, not to quiet / loud. Modern German uses stimmlos / stimmhaft.
inlautend
Inside a word. A word-initial fricative is not licensed for this voicing simply because its word is unaccented.
betonter silben
Accented syllables. The immediately preceding syllable matters; an accent somewhere earlier in the word is not enough.

A deliberately invented word / p. 114

Ein fingirtes indogermanisches wort *akasatam entwickelte sich auf germanischem gebiete erst zu … je nachdem der accent auf der ersten, zweiten, dritten oder vierten silbe ruhte.

An invented Indo-European word *akasatam developed in the Germanic area first into … according to whether the accent rested on the first, second, third, or fourth syllable.

fingirtes
Invented, hypothetical. This word is a controlled thought experiment in Verner's article, not a recovered ancient word.
je nachdem
Depending on whether. The omitted middle contains his phonetic notation and alternatives; see the complete page and the continuation on p. 115.

A rule has to travel beyond its first examples / p. 117 / cited

Soll die regel allgemeine gültigkeit haben, so muss sie auch die differenzirung in allen übrigen fällen erklären können

If the rule is to have general validity, it must also be able to explain the differentiation in all the other cases.

allgemeine gültigkeit
General validity. Matching the starting pair is weaker than accounting for new material. Even eight comparisons do not establish a universal historical claim.
übrigen fällen
The remaining cases. Verner derived his account from verbal alternations before extending it to vocabulary and endings. This workshop reverses that teaching order.

Keep the resistant evidence / p. 119 / cited

Von wörtern, bei denen die regel nicht passt, habe ich folgende notirt:

Of words for which the rule does not fit, I have noted the following:

nicht passt
Does not fit. The following list includes katará- beside Gothic hvaþar, and páti- beside the compound member -fadi-. The comparison's difficulty is part of the evidence.
notirt
Recorded; modern spelling notiert. An acknowledged mismatch is not permission to edit an observed form or assign an unattested accent without an argument.

Accent need not be loudness / p. 115

Entweder geschieht das hervorheben einer silbe dadurch, dass die stimmbänder stärker gespannt werden; es entsteht dadurch ein höherer ton dem niedrigeren tone der unaccentuirten silben gegenüber.

Either a syllable is made prominent by the vocal folds being tightened more strongly; this produces a higher pitch compared with the lower pitch of the unaccented syllables.

höherer ton
Higher pitch. Verner's footnote distinguishes pitch from greater force. The movable mark in this workshop represents position, not a recording or a reconstruction of accent's acoustic realization.
accentus / προσῳδία
Verner cites these Latin and Greek names in the same note. Greek προσῳδία gives English prosody. Their presence does not make Sanskrit, Latin, or Greek the parent of Gothic.

The earlier accent leaves evidence / p. 130

Wenn idg. k t p im inlaute sich im germanischen bald als h þ f, bald als g d b wiederfinden, so ist dies durch jene ältere accentuation bedingt.

When Indo-European k t p inside a word appear in Germanic sometimes as h þ f, sometimes as g d b, this is conditioned by that earlier accentuation.

jene ältere accentuation
That earlier accentuation. Later accent position can conceal the conditioning of an earlier change. This is an inference from comparative evidence, not a sound recording.
idg.
Indogermanisch, Indo-European. This is a historical language-family label. It is not a classification of people's genomes or ethnic identities.

Inferring the older accent

This is an inverse experiment on the fictional word. Question marks withhold a consonant; a fitting scenario is not necessarily uniquely identified.

Consonant evidence: g / z / þ. Either event order allowed.

Only older accent position 3 fits the selected evidence in this model.

Position 4First-syllable accent fixed first*ahazad(am)First consonant: evidence g, model h. Third consonant: evidence þ, model d.

Last checked proposal

Position 3; evidence g / z / þ; Either event order allowed.

Position 3 is the only older accent compatible with the selected evidence and order assumption. This result belongs to Verner's fictional word.

This check keeps its own evidence and order assumption when the controls change.

The saved environment test

Word-initial: no; voiced neighbors: yes; immediately preceding syllable accented: yes.

θ becomes θ. The immediately preceding syllable bears the older accent.

What this evidence can support

This is a deliberately small, selected comparison set, not a representative sample or a proof of a sound law. The resistant rows are retained. Sanskrit accent may have its own history; analogy, compounds, inflection, and other changes need separate evidence. This is a study of language histories, not ancestry or identity of peoples.

The underlying sequence begins with an assumed inherited dental; it does not derive Gothic from Sanskrit or Latin. Later English developments are outside the model. No recorded pronunciation or ancient acoustic reconstruction is supplied.

Complete source pages

Karl Verner, Eine ausnahme der ersten lautverschiebung, Zeitschrift für vergleichende Sprachforschung 23 (1877), pp. 97–130. Signed Copenhagen, July 1875. Original volume; 1967 translation for comparison (not reproduced here).
